lessons.title: Lesson 1: What automation and AI workflows are
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain triggers, actions and where an AI step fits.
This lesson builds toward: Given an everyday automation, you will identify its trigger, its actions and where an AI step fits, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Every automation has the same shape. A trigger is the event that starts it: a form is submitted, an email arrives, a date comes. Actions are what happens next: add a row to a spreadsheet, send an email, create a task.
Plain automation follows fixed rules: if a form arrives, copy it to the sheet. An AI step adds judgment-like work: read a message and decide if it is a complaint, a question or a sales lead; summarize it in two sentences; draft a polite reply.
Different tools use different names. Zapier calls an automation a Zap, Power Automate calls it a flow, and Make calls it a scenario. The idea is the same: when this happens, do that.
Words to know:
- Automation: software doing steps for you without a person each time.
- Trigger: the event that starts an automation.
- Action: a step the automation does after the trigger.
- Workflow: the series of steps used to get a task done.
Try it now: Write three "when this happens, do that" automations you wish you had at work, home or a group you belong to. Circle the one that could use an AI step.
You can now describe any automation as a trigger plus actions, and say where AI could help.

check.q: What does Power Automate call an automation?
check.why: Power Automate calls it a flow; Zapier calls it a Zap and Make calls it a scenario.

check.q: You want each new message sorted as a complaint, question or sales lead. Which part does that?
check.why: Reading a message and sorting it is judgment-like work for an AI step.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Mapping a workflow and finding what to automate
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Map a repeated task step by step and pick the steps to automate.
This lesson builds toward: For a task done at least weekly, you will map each step with who, which tool and how long, and mark each step automate, AI draft plus human check, or keep human, with an estimate of time saved each week.
Before you build, map the task as it is done today. Write each step, who does it, which tool they use and how long it takes. A volunteer sign-up might be: read the email, copy details to a spreadsheet, check the schedule, send a welcome email, add a calendar reminder.
Good steps to automate are repeated, rule-based and boring: copying, filing, reminding, confirming. Steps that need judgment, kindness or a decision about someone's life should stay with a person, or use AI only to draft.
Mark each step: automate, AI draft with human check, or keep human. That marked map is your design.
Step by step:
- Pick a task done at least weekly.
- Write each step in order, with who, which tool and how long.
- Mark each step: automate, AI draft plus human check, or keep human.
- Estimate the time saved each week.
Words to know:
- Workflow map: a step-by-step list or drawing of how a task gets done.
- Human in the loop: a person checks or approves before the automation continues.
Try it now: Map one repeated task with at least five steps. Mark each step automate, AI draft plus human check, or keep human, and estimate weekly time saved.
You can now map a workflow and decide which steps to automate, which AI can draft and which stay human.

check.q: Which step is a good candidate to fully automate?
options: Adding a calendar reminder after sign-up
check.why: Repeated, rule-based steps like reminders are good to automate.

check.q: Your map includes "reply to a family asking for help with rent". How do you mark it?
options: AI draft plus human check, or keep human
check.why: Steps that need kindness or affect someone's life stay with a person, or AI only drafts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Designing the automation on paper
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a full automation design: trigger, actions, AI prompt, checks and data rules.
This lesson builds toward: Before using any tool, you will write an automation design with the trigger, actions, AI prompt, human checkpoints and data rules, with a human approval wherever a mistake would hurt.
Design on paper before touching a tool. Write the trigger, each action in order, and the exact AI prompt if there is an AI step, for example: "Read this request. Reply with one word: Quote, Question or Complaint. Then write a two-sentence summary."
Add a human checkpoint wherever a mistake would hurt: anything sent to a customer, money moved, or a decision about a person. The automation can draft and then wait for approval.
Write data rules: what information flows through the automation, where it is stored, and what must never pass through an AI step, such as card numbers, Social Security numbers, health details or passwords. Check what each connected tool does with your data.
Step by step:
- Write the trigger.
- List each action in order.
- Write the exact AI prompt for any AI step.
- Add a human approval where mistakes would hurt.
- Write the data rules: what flows, where it is stored, what never goes through AI.
Words to know:
- Prompt: the instruction you give an AI step.
- Checkpoint: a point where a person reviews before the automation continues.
Try it now: Write a one-page design for your automation: trigger, actions, AI prompt, human checkpoint and data rules.
You can now design an automation with an AI step, a human checkpoint and safe data rules.

check.q: What do data rules in a design say?
options: What flows, where it is stored and what never goes through AI
check.why: Data rules cover what information flows, where it is stored and what never passes through AI.

check.q: Your automation will send replies to customers. Where do you add a human checkpoint?
options: Before the reply is sent, so a person approves the draft
check.why: Anything sent to a customer should wait for a person's approval.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Building, testing and running it

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building your first automation
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a simple automation from a form to a spreadsheet to an email.
This lesson builds toward: Using a form, a spreadsheet and a no-code tool, you will build an automation that saves responses, runs an AI step and sends a draft for approval, so the basic flow works before the AI step is added.
Start with the simplest version that works. Google Forms can save every response to a Google Sheet without any extra tool, and Microsoft Forms can send responses to Excel. That alone is an automation.
To add actions, use a no-code tool such as Zapier, Power Automate or Make. Most have free plans or trials with limits; check each tool's pricing page, since plans change. Connect your accounts, choose the trigger (new form response or new spreadsheet row), then add actions (send an email, create a task).
Add the AI step last, once the basic flow works. Many tools have a built-in AI action or connect to an AI service. Paste in the prompt from your design and send its result to the next action, such as a draft email that waits for a person to approve.
Step by step:
- Make a form with the fields you need.
- Link it to a spreadsheet.
- In a no-code tool, set the trigger: new response or new row.
- Add an action: send an email or create a task.
- Add the AI step with your prompt, sending its result to a draft for approval.
Words to know:
- No-code tool: software that lets you build without writing code.
- Connect: give one app permission to work with another.
- Field: one question or box in a form.
Official sources:
- Zapier
- Microsoft Power Automate
- Make
Try it now: Build the first part of your automation: a form linked to a spreadsheet. If you can, add one action in a no-code tool, such as an email to yourself for each new response.
You can now build a basic form-to-spreadsheet-to-email automation in no-code tools.

check.q: Which simple setup is already an automation with no extra tool?
options: Microsoft Forms sending responses to Excel
Typing form answers into a sheet by hand
check.why: Microsoft Forms can send responses to Excel automatically.

check.q: Your basic form-to-email flow works. What do you add next?
options: The AI step with the prompt from your design
check.why: Add the AI step last, once the basic flow works.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Testing with sample data
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Test an automation with normal and tricky sample entries and fix what breaks.
This lesson builds toward: Given your built automation, you will test it with five sample entries, including tricky ones, and fix what breaks, using only made-up data, with every failure fixed and re-tested.
Never turn on an automation for real people until it passes tests. Use made-up sample entries, not real customer data.
Test five cases: a normal entry, a blank field, a very long message, a misspelled or unusual entry, and one the AI step might sort wrongly. Check each step: did the row appear, did the email go to the right place, did the AI sort and summarize correctly?
Write a test log: input, expected result, actual result, pass or fail, fix. Common fixes: make a form field required, tighten the AI prompt ("Reply with exactly one word"), or add a filter so only certain entries continue.
Step by step:
- Write five sample entries, including tricky ones.
- Run each through the automation.
- Check every step's result.
- Record pass or fail in a test log.
- Fix and re-test the failures.
Words to know:
- Test case: one sample input used to check that something works.
- Filter: a rule that lets only certain items continue in an automation.
Try it now: Run five sample entries through your automation, including at least two tricky ones. Record a test log and fix one problem.
You can now test an automation with sample data, log results and fix what fails.

check.q: What goes in an automation test log?
options: Input, expected result, actual result, pass or fail, and fix
check.why: A test log records what went in, what should happen, what did, and the fix.

check.q: A test entry with a blank email field breaks the flow. What is a common fix?
options: Make the email field required on the form
Use real customer data to test
check.why: Making the field required stops blank entries from breaking the flow.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Running, monitoring and improving
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn the automation on safely, watch it, and know what to do when it fails.
This lesson builds toward: When the automation goes live, you will monitor the run history, set an error alert, name an owner and write a one-page instruction sheet, so someone else could run or turn it off.
Turn it on for a small group first, such as one form or one week. Check the results daily at the start. Most tools show a run history that lists each run and whether it succeeded.
Automations break: a password changes, a field gets renamed, a free plan hits its limit, or the AI step starts sorting oddly. Set up an error alert to your email, and name an owner who checks it.
Write a one-page instruction sheet: what the automation does, where it lives, who owns it and how to turn it off. If the owner leaves, someone else can keep it running. Review it every few months and ask: is it still saving time?
Step by step:
- Turn it on for a small group or one week.
- Check the run history daily at first.
- Set an error alert and name an owner.
- Write a one-page instruction sheet.
- Review every few months.
Words to know:
- Run history: a list of each time an automation ran and whether it worked.
- Error alert: a message telling you an automation failed.
Try it now: Final task: finish your automation with its AI step and human approval, run five test entries, then write the one-page instruction sheet with the workflow map, trigger and actions, test results and owner.
You can now design, build, test and run an AI-powered automation with a person in control.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Workflow map Steps are missing, or no step is marked. Each step with who, tool and time, marked automate, AI draft plus human check, or keep human. Includes an estimate of time saved each week. Trigger, actions and AI step The automation does not run from its trigger, or the AI step is missing. A working trigger, actions in order and an AI step that summarizes and sorts the request. Uses a filter or a tight one-word prompt so results are consistent. Human check and data rules Replies go out with no approval, or private data passes through the AI step. A person approves the draft reply, and data rules say what never goes through AI. Notes what each connected tool does with the data. Five test runs Fewer than five tests, real data used, or failures not fixed. Five made-up test entries, including tricky ones, logged with pass or fail and fixes. Every failure was re-tested and passed. Owner and instructions No named owner or instructions. A named owner, an error alert and a one-page instruction sheet. The sheet says how to turn it off and when it will be reviewed. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does an error alert do?
options: Emails the owner when a run fails
check.why: An error alert tells the owner right away when something breaks.

check.q: The person who built your automation is leaving. What keeps it running?
options: A one-page instruction sheet and a new owner who checks alerts
Changing all the passwords and telling no one
check.why: The instruction sheet and a named owner let someone else run or turn it off.
